title: India, China and the Silk Roads
bigQuestion: How did the empires of India and China govern millions of people, and how did goods and ideas travel between worlds that never met face to face?

story.title: Silk Out, Glass Home
story.kicker: Around the year 100, a caravan leaves the Han capital for the west, carrying cloth that the Romans will pay for in gold.
paragraphs: Before dawn, the western gate of Chang'an is already loud. Chang'an is the capital of Han China, one of the largest cities in the world, laid out in a grid of walled wards. A merchant named Lu checks the loads on forty camels. Each carries bolts of silk, packed in oiled cloth against the rain. Silk is made from the cocoons of moths fed on mulberry leaves, and how to make it is a secret the Chinese have kept for centuries. Lu also carries bronze mirrors and lacquered boxes.

The caravan will not go to Rome. No single trader ever did. Lu will travel for months along the Gansu corridor, a strip of grassland between mountains and desert, past the last Chinese fort. There, in an oasis town, he will sell his silk to Sogdian merchants from central Asia. They will carry it over mountains to Persia. Persians will sell it to Greeks and Syrians, who will ship it across the Mediterranean. By the time a Roman woman wears it, the silk has changed hands a dozen times and its price has multiplied.

The road is dangerous. The Taklamakan Desert is so dry that caravans hug its edges from oasis to oasis. Bandits wait in the passes. Camels can go days without water and can smell it from far off, which is why Lu trusts them more than horses. At night the drivers sleep in walled rest stops, where Lu hears languages he does not know and sees priests of religions he has never met.

At the oasis market, Lu trades. He takes back things China cannot make or grow: glass bowls from Roman Syria, so clear they seem like frozen water, wool carpets, grapes and walnuts, a horse from the Ferghana valley that his emperor's army prizes. He also takes back stories. A Buddhist monk from India asks to travel with the caravan east. Lu agrees. The monk carries scrolls of teaching that will change China more than any glass bowl.

Months later Lu rides back through the western gate of Chang'an. He has never left the lands between China and Persia, yet his silk is now in Rome and Rome's glass is on his camel. Historians call this web of routes the Silk Roads. It carried cloth, spices, paper, religions, inventions and, sometimes, deadly disease, across the whole of Eurasia.
story.think: No one traveled the whole Silk Road, yet goods and ideas crossed it. What does that tell you about how connected the ancient world really was?

lessons.title: The Maurya Empire and Ashoka
lessons.mainIdea: The Maurya dynasty united most of India, and its greatest king, Ashoka, gave up conquest for a rule based on compassion.
reading: Northern India is a land of great rivers, the Indus in the west and the Ganges in the east, watered by summer monsoon rains. By 500 BCE it held many small kingdoms and republics. Not long after Alexander the Great reached the Indus and turned back, a young leader named Chandragupta Maurya seized the kingdom of Magadha on the Ganges, around 321 BCE. He built the *Maurya Empire*, the first to rule most of the Indian subcontinent.

The Mauryan state was well organized. A minister's handbook from the period describes spies, tax collectors, roads with rest houses and a huge army. The capital, Pataliputra, had wooden walls with hundreds of towers. A Greek ambassador who visited wrote about its size and order, though his book survives only in pieces quoted by others.

Chandragupta's grandson *Ashoka* came to the throne around 268 BCE. Early in his reign he conquered the coastal kingdom of Kalinga in a war that, by his own account, killed and displaced hundreds of thousands of people. Ashoka said the suffering horrified him. He turned to Buddhism and announced that he would rule by *dharma*, a word meaning right conduct and duty.

How do we know? Ashoka had his messages carved on rocks and tall polished stone pillars across his empire, in local languages. More than thirty of these edicts survive. In them he urges kindness to servants and animals, respect for all religions, and planting shade trees and wells along the roads. He sent Buddhist missionaries as far as Sri Lanka and the Greek kingdoms. After his death around 232 BCE, the empire weakened and broke apart within about fifty years.

words.d: the first empire to rule most of India, founded by Chandragupta about 321 BCE
Mauryan emperor who turned from conquest to Buddhist rule around 260 BCE
in Indian thought, right conduct and duty; Ashoka's word for how he tried to rule
an official order or message from a ruler, in Ashoka's case carved on rock and stone pillars

look.title: Ashoka Regrets a War
look.text: In one rock edict, the king says that eight years after his coronation he conquered Kalinga. A hundred and fifty thousand people were carried away, a hundred thousand were killed and many more died. Afterward, he says, he felt deep sorrow, because the conquest of a free people brings slaughter and the loss of loved ones. Now, he says, he wishes all beings to be safe and would rather win people by dharma than by force.
look.cite: Ashoka, Thirteenth Rock Edict, about 260 BCE (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Ashoka published his own regret for all to read. Why might a ruler do that? What does it tell us that we should still be cautious about?

check.q: What was new about the Maurya Empire?
choices: It was the first Buddhist kingdom
It was the first empire to rule most of India
check.why: Chandragupta Maurya built the first empire covering most of the Indian subcontinent around 321 BCE.

check.q: What changed Ashoka's way of ruling?
choices: The suffering caused by his conquest of Kalinga
check.why: By his own account, the deaths in the Kalinga war horrified him, and he turned to Buddhism and rule by dharma.

check.q: What is the main source for what Ashoka believed?
choices: His own edicts carved on rocks and pillars
check.why: More than thirty of Ashoka's carved messages survive, in his own words.

lessons.title: Hinduism and Buddhism
lessons.mainIdea: Hinduism grew from ancient Indian traditions of many gods, duty and rebirth, and Buddhism arose within that world as a path to end suffering.
reading: *Hinduism* is not one founder's religion. It grew over thousands of years from the hymns of the Vedas, composed by about 1500 to 1000 BCE, and from later teachings. Hindus honor many gods, such as Vishnu the preserver and Shiva the destroyer, often as faces of one ultimate reality called Brahman. Two ideas shape Hindu life. *Karma* means that every action has consequences that follow a person. *Reincarnation* means the soul is reborn in new bodies, and good karma leads to a better rebirth.

Indian society was divided into groups by birth, later called castes: priests, warriors and rulers, merchants and farmers, and laborers, with others considered outside the system altogether. Hindu teaching linked each group to its own dharma, or duty. This gave order, but it also locked people into place. Reformers, then and now, have challenged it.

Around 500 BCE a prince named Siddhartha Gautama, born near the border of today's India and Nepal, left his palace after seeing sickness, old age and death. After years of searching he sat under a tree and, his followers say, reached enlightenment. He became the *Buddha*, the awakened one. He taught that life involves suffering, that suffering comes from craving, that craving can be ended, and that the way is a middle path of right living, meditation and wisdom.

*Buddhism* accepted karma and rebirth but rejected the caste system and the need for priests. Anyone could follow the path. Monks and nuns organized communities, and rulers like Ashoka spread the teaching. Over centuries Buddhism reached Sri Lanka, central Asia, China, Korea and Japan, while in India itself Hinduism remained the faith of most people. Both religions are alive today with hundreds of millions of followers, including many in the Chicago area.

words.d: the ancient religion of India with many gods, karma, rebirth and duty
the idea that every action brings results that follow a person into this life and the next
the belief that the soul is reborn in a new body after death
the awakened one; the title of Siddhartha Gautama, who taught a path out of suffering
the religion based on the Buddha's teaching of the middle path

look.title: The Prince at the Gate
look.text: A young prince has everything: a palace, a family, servants who keep anything unpleasant out of sight. One day he rides out and sees an old man bent with age, then a sick man, then a funeral. He has never seen these things before. That night he cannot sleep.
look.prompt: Why would seeing ordinary suffering change a person's whole life? What questions would you start asking?

check.q: What does karma mean?
choices: Actions bring consequences that follow a person
check.why: Karma is the idea that every action has results, shaping this life and the next.

check.q: How did Buddhism differ from the Hindu society around it?
choices: It rejected the caste system and priests
It allowed only princes to follow it
check.why: Buddhism kept karma and rebirth but opened its path to anyone regardless of birth.

check.q: According to the Buddha, where does suffering come from?
choices: Being born in a low caste
check.why: The Buddha taught that suffering comes from craving and can be ended by following the middle path.

lessons.title: The Gupta Age and the Zero
lessons.mainIdea: Under the Gupta empire India produced great art, literature and the number system with zero that the whole world now uses.
reading: About five hundred years after the Mauryas fell, another family united northern India. The *Gupta Empire* lasted from about 320 to 550 CE. It was smaller than Ashoka's and its kings let local rulers keep much of their power. But it was peaceful and rich, and historians often call it India's classical age. A Chinese Buddhist monk named Faxian who traveled there around 400 CE wrote that the people were prosperous and the roads safe.

Gupta artists carved stone temples and painted cave walls, and poets wrote in Sanskrit, the classical language of India. The playwright Kalidasa wrote dramas still performed today. Buddhist monasteries such as Nalanda grew into universities that drew students from across Asia. Doctors performed surgery and described many diseases.

The greatest Gupta gift was mathematics. Indian scholars developed a *decimal* system with ten digits, in which a digit's value depends on its place, and they used a symbol for *zero*. That last step sounds small. It was enormous. With zero as a placeholder, you can tell 205 from 25, and with zero as a number, you can subtract, multiply and build algebra. The Romans, with their numerals, could barely multiply.

The astronomer Aryabhata, around 500 CE, calculated the length of the year and the value of pi with great accuracy and argued that the Earth turns on its axis. Indian numbers traveled west to Arab scholars, who spread them to Europe, which is why we call them Arabic numerals. Every time you write a 0, you use an idea from Gupta India.

words.d: the empire in northern India from about 320 to 550 CE, known as India's classical age
a number system based on ten, in which a digit's value depends on its place
the number and placeholder symbol that Indian mathematicians developed

look.title: Writing Numbers Two Ways
look.cite: count of characters in each notation
look.prompt: Try multiplying CCCLXXXVIII by VII without converting. Why does place value with a zero make arithmetic so much easier?

check.q: How do we know about daily life under the Guptas?
choices: From the account of a visiting Chinese monk, Faxian
check.why: Faxian traveled through Gupta India around 400 CE and described prosperous, safe conditions.

check.q: Why does a zero matter in a place-value system?
choices: Without it you cannot tell 205 from 25
It was required by the Gupta kings
check.why: Zero holds a place so that each digit's position gives its value, which makes arithmetic possible.

check.q: Why are Indian numerals called Arabic numerals in the West?
choices: Because Arab scholars carried them from India to Europe
Because they were invented in Arabia
check.why: Arab mathematicians adopted the Indian system and passed it on to Europe, which named it after them.

lessons.title: The First Emperor
lessons.mainIdea: In 221 BCE the king of Qin conquered the warring states of China and ruled by harsh laws and strict standardization.
reading: For centuries, China was split among rival kingdoms that fought endlessly, a period known as the Warring States. One of them, *Qin*, in the west, had rebuilt itself around a philosophy called *Legalism*. Legalists believed people were selfish and had to be controlled by strict laws, heavy punishments and rewards. Qin's armies were large and disciplined, and its king was ruthless.

By 221 BCE he had crushed every rival and united China for the first time. He gave himself a new title, *Shi Huangdi*, First Emperor, and expected his family to rule for ten thousand generations. Our word China probably comes from Qin. He divided the land into districts run by officials he appointed, not by nobles who inherited power.

The First Emperor made everything the same. One system of writing, so officials anywhere could read orders. One set of weights and measures, one coin with a square hole, and even one axle width for carts so that all wheels fit the same ruts. He built roads and canals and forced hundreds of thousands of laborers to work on them. He linked older walls in the north into a long barrier against nomadic raiders, an early version of the Great Wall.

He also feared ideas. Traditional accounts say he ordered books of history and philosophy burned, keeping only useful ones on farming and medicine, and had scholars who resisted executed. He searched for a potion of eternal life and may have died from one. When he died in 210 BCE, revolts broke out at once. The Qin dynasty lasted only four years more. Yet the unified empire it built lasted, in one form or another, for two thousand years.

words.d: the western Chinese state that conquered its rivals and united China in 221 BCE
a Chinese philosophy holding that people must be controlled by strict laws and punishments
First Emperor, the title taken by the ruler of Qin
to make things the same everywhere, such as writing, coins and measures

look.title: One Width for Every Wheel
look.text: Before Qin, a cart from one kingdom could not use the deep ruts worn by carts of another, because the wheels were set at different widths. After the First Emperor's order, every cart in China was built to one width. A load of grain could roll from the coast to the far west without changing wagons.
look.prompt: What other things does a modern country standardize so that people far apart can work together? What is gained and what is lost?

check.q: What did Legalists believe about people?
choices: They are naturally good and need little government
They are selfish and must be controlled by strict laws
They should choose their own rulers
They should follow the Buddha's path
check.why: Legalism held that only harsh laws, punishments and rewards could keep order.

check.q: Why did the First Emperor create one system of writing for all China?
choices: To make books easier to burn
So officials everywhere could read and carry out his orders
Because Qin had no writing before
check.why: Standard writing, coins and measures let a single government run a huge land.

check.q: What happened to the Qin dynasty after the First Emperor died in 210 BCE?
choices: It ruled for ten thousand generations
It moved the capital to India
It collapsed within a few years amid revolts
check.why: Harsh rule bred rebellion, and the dynasty fell by 206 BCE, though the unified empire survived under the Han.

lessons.title: The Clay Army
lessons.mainIdea: The First Emperor's tomb, guarded by thousands of life-size clay soldiers, shows both his power and the labor it cost.
reading: In 1974 farmers near the city of Xi'an were digging a well in a dry season. They hit pieces of hardened clay shaped like a man. Archaeologists came and began to dig. They uncovered pits holding an army of *terracotta*, baked clay, soldiers standing in battle formation. So far about eight thousand figures have been found: infantry, archers, charioteers, officers, horses. Each is life-size, and no two faces are the same.

The soldiers guard the tomb of the First Emperor, a mound about a mile away that has never been opened. An ancient historian, Sima Qian, wrote a century later that the tomb held a model of the empire with rivers of flowing mercury and that the craftsmen who built it were sealed inside so its secrets would die with them. Tests of the soil have found unusually high mercury levels, which suggests his account may contain truth.

The figures were once painted in bright colors and held real bronze weapons, some still sharp. Workers made them in an assembly line: legs, bodies, arms and heads molded separately, then joined and finished by hand. Stamps on the clay give the names of the workshops and foremen who were responsible for quality. Sima Qian says seven hundred thousand laborers worked on the tomb complex, a figure historians treat as very rough.

The terracotta army is evidence in several ways. It shows how Qin soldiers dressed, stood and were armed. It shows the emperor's belief that he would rule in the next world as in this one. And it shows the cost of that belief: a generation of forced labor for a single man's tomb. The same power that standardized carts and writing could also consume the lives of its people.

words.d: baked clay, used for pottery and for the First Emperor's soldiers
Chinese historian of the Han dynasty, about 100 BCE, who wrote the first full history of China
the study of the past through objects and remains dug from the ground

look.title: The First Emperor's Army
rows: Terracotta figures found so far, about
Years the Qin dynasty lasted, about
look.cite: Chinese archaeological reports, rounded; standard dates
look.prompt: Eight thousand figures were made in about eleven years of the emperor's rule. What does that tell you about how the Qin state organized work?

check.q: How was the terracotta army discovered?
choices: Sima Qian's book gave its location
Farmers digging a well hit clay figures in 1974
The emperor's tomb was opened in 1900
Soldiers found it while building the Great Wall
check.why: Local farmers struck pieces of a clay figure while digging a well, and archaeologists took over.

check.q: Which evidence supports Sima Qian's story of rivers of mercury in the tomb?
choices: The tomb has been fully excavated
The clay soldiers are painted silver
Soil tests show high mercury levels near the mound
The farmers found mercury in the well
check.why: The tomb is unopened, but unusually high mercury in the soil suggests the story may be true.

choices: The army used only stone weapons
The state could organize huge forced labor for the emperor's wishes
check.why: Assembly-line production and stamped workshop names show a tightly organized labor system built on forced work.

lessons.title: The Han and Confucius
lessons.mainIdea: The Han dynasty ruled China for four centuries by blending strong government with Confucian ideas of duty, learning and fair rule.
reading: After Qin fell, a peasant-born rebel leader named Liu Bang won the wars that followed and founded the *Han dynasty* in 206 BCE. It lasted, with one short break, until 220 CE, about four hundred years. The Han kept the Qin's unified empire, districts and officials, but softened the laws. Chinese people today still call themselves Han.

The Han turned to an older thinker for ideas about how to rule well. *Confucius* had lived around 551 to 479 BCE, in the Warring States period, and had failed to find a ruler who would take his advice. His students wrote down his sayings. He taught that society works when everyone fulfills the duties of their role: rulers should be just and set a good example, officials honest, children respectful of parents, and all people should study and improve themselves.

This was *Confucianism*. It said a ruler held power by the Mandate of Heaven, the approval of the heavens, which could be withdrawn if he ruled badly, and floods, famines and revolts were signs of that. So a wise emperor listened to his advisers and cared for his people. The Han emperor Wudi, who ruled from 141 to 87 BCE, made Confucian teaching the official learning of the state and set up an imperial academy to train officials in it.

Han China was, alongside Rome, one of the two great powers of the ancient world. The two empires each had about sixty million people at their height. They knew of each other only faintly. The Han pushed their control west into central Asia to protect the trade routes, expanded south and fought long wars against the Xiongnu nomads on the northern steppe. Sima Qian, the court historian, wrote a history of China from its legendary beginnings to his own day.

words.d: the Chinese ruling family from 206 BCE to 220 CE
Chinese teacher, about 551 to 479 BCE, whose ideas about duty and good rule shaped China
the philosophy that order comes from everyone fulfilling the duties of their role, starting with a just ruler
the idea that heaven approves a just ruler and withdraws support from a bad one

look.title: Sayings of Confucius
look.text: Confucius, his students recorded, was asked about government and answered that it means enough food, enough soldiers and the trust of the people. Asked which to give up first, he said soldiers, then food, for if the people do not trust their rulers, the state cannot stand. Elsewhere he said: do not do to others what you would not want done to yourself.
look.cite: The Analects of Confucius, compiled by his followers after 479 BCE (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Confucius put the people's trust above the army. Compare that with the Legalist view that people must be controlled by fear. Which do you think works better, and when?

check.q: How did the Han differ from the Qin?
choices: They kept the unified empire but softened the harsh laws
They broke China back into warring states
check.why: The Han kept Qin's structure of districts and appointed officials but ruled with less cruelty and used Confucian ideas.

check.q: According to Confucius, what makes a society work well?
choices: Everyone fulfilling the duties of their role, beginning with a just ruler
check.why: Confucius taught that rulers, officials, parents and children each have duties, and order flows from doing them.

check.q: What would a flood or famine mean under the idea of the Mandate of Heaven?
choices: Heaven might be withdrawing its approval of a bad ruler
check.why: Disasters were read as signs that heaven's approval of the ruler was in doubt, a warning to rule better.

lessons.title: Paper and the Civil Service
lessons.mainIdea: Han China invented paper and began choosing officials by examination, two ideas that spread around the world.
reading: Before paper, Chinese writing went on strips of bamboo tied with cord, heavy and bulky, or on silk, which was costly. Around 105 CE a court official named Cai Lun is credited with reporting a new method to the emperor. Workers mashed tree bark, old rags, hemp and fishing nets into a pulp, spread it thin on a screen, and let it dry into a sheet. *Paper* was cheap, light and easy to write on. Archaeologists have found even older scraps, so Cai Lun probably improved a process already in use.

Paper changed everything a government does. Records, tax rolls, maps and letters could be made and stored in quantity. Books multiplied. Centuries later the Chinese would add printing. Paper spread slowly along the Silk Roads to central Asia, reached the Arab world by the 700s and Europe by around 1100. Every page you read on paper began in Han China.

The Han also faced a question every large state faces: how do you pick honest, capable officials? The Qin had appointed loyal men. The Han began to ask local leaders to recommend people of good character and to test them on Confucian learning. The imperial academy trained thousands of students. Over later dynasties this grew into the *civil service* examination, a set of written tests open, in theory, to any man who could study, which decided who governed.

The examination system had limits. Studying took years and money, so most winners came from families that could afford it, and women were excluded. But the idea that officials should earn their post by knowledge, not birth, was powerful. In the 1800s Britain and then the United States copied it. When someone in Illinois takes a test to become a state employee, they are following a Han idea.

words.d: a writing material made from plant fibers mashed into pulp and dried in sheets, invented in Han China
the officials who run a government's daily work; in China they were chosen by examination
earning a position by ability and knowledge rather than by birth or connections

rows: Papermaking in the Arab world, about (CE)
look.prompt: About how many years did paper take to reach Europe from China? Why might a useful invention travel so slowly?

check.q: What was the main advantage of paper over bamboo strips and silk?
choices: It was cheap, light and easy to write on
It was made only for the emperor
check.why: Paper made from bark, rags and nets was inexpensive and light, so records and books could multiply.

check.q: Why does the lesson say Cai Lun probably improved rather than invented paper?
choices: Older scraps of paper have been found by archaeologists
check.why: Scraps older than 105 CE exist, so paper was already in use and Cai Lun likely refined the method.

check.q: What was the key idea behind the Chinese examination system?
choices: Officials should be chosen by their fathers
Officials should earn their posts by knowledge, not birth
check.why: The examinations aimed to choose officials by merit, an idea later copied by Britain and the United States.

lessons.title: Routes and Goods
lessons.mainIdea: The Silk Roads were a web of land and sea routes across Eurasia along which goods passed through many hands between China, India, Persia and Rome.
reading: There was never one silk road. The name was invented by a German geographer in the 1800s for a network of routes that connected China with the Mediterranean. The main land routes ran west from Chang'an through the Gansu corridor, split around the Taklamakan Desert, crossed the Pamir Mountains and continued through Persia to Syria. Sea routes joined southern China, Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and Egypt with the monsoon winds.

The Han opened the western routes on purpose. Around 138 BCE the emperor Wudi sent an envoy named Zhang Qian west to find allies against the Xiongnu. He was captured and held for years, escaped and came home with reports of rich kingdoms and fine horses in the Ferghana valley. Han armies followed, set up forts and made the roads safer. Trade grew.

Goods flowed both ways. From China came *silk*, lacquerware, bronze mirrors and later paper and porcelain. From India came cotton cloth, pepper and other spices, ivory and gems. From Persia and Rome came glass, wool, horses, wine, silver coins and gold. Rome's writers grumbled that the empire was pouring gold into Asia to pay for luxuries. Along the way, oasis cities such as Samarkand and Kashgar grew rich as middlemen.

Almost no merchant traveled the whole distance. Goods passed from Chinese to Sogdian to Persian to Greek traders, each adding a markup. Silk that cost little in China was, by some ancient accounts, worth its weight in gold in Rome. Rome and China each knew the other existed and sent envoys that never quite arrived. A Chinese record describes a Roman embassy reaching the Han court in 166 CE, though scholars think it may have been a group of merchants claiming official status.

words.d: the network of land and sea trade routes linking China, India, Persia and the Mediterranean
fine cloth made from silkworm cocoons; China kept the method secret for centuries
Han envoy sent west around 138 BCE whose reports opened the trade routes
a trader who buys goods from one party and sells them to another, taking a profit

lessons.title: Ideas on the Move
lessons.mainIdea: Religions, inventions and knowledge traveled the Silk Roads with the traders, changing every society they reached.
reading: Merchants carried more than cloth. A trader who spent a season in an oasis town heard new prayers, saw new tools and tasted new foods. The most important traveler on the Silk Roads was not a good at all. It was *Buddhism*. Monks from India walked east with the caravans, and by the first century CE Buddhist communities existed in China. Over the next centuries Chinese pilgrims, including Faxian, made the reverse trip to India to collect scriptures.

Buddhism changed as it traveled. Along the routes, in what is now Afghanistan and Pakistan, artists influenced by Greek sculpture carved the first statues of the Buddha in human form. In China, Buddhism mixed with local ideas and grew into new schools. Cave temples cut into cliffs along the routes, such as those at Dunhuang, hold thousands of painted walls and manuscripts that show this blending. From China, Buddhism went on to Korea and Japan.

Other faiths traveled too: Christianity, Zoroastrianism from Persia, Judaism, and later Islam. Technology moved as well. Paper went west. The crossbow, the stirrup and methods of making iron and steel spread. Crops crossed between regions: grapes, walnuts and alfalfa came east to China, while peaches and apricots, native to China, went west and were later called Persian by the Romans.

Knowledge crossed as well. Indian numbers, including zero, went west with traders and scholars. Greek astronomy reached India. Chinese silk-making itself finally escaped, the story goes, when silkworm eggs were smuggled to the Byzantine Empire in the 500s CE. The Silk Roads show that no civilization built itself alone. Each borrowed, adapted and passed things on.

words.d: a person who travels a long way for a religious purpose
an oasis on the Silk Roads in western China with painted Buddhist cave temples
the spread of ideas, customs and technology from one society to another

look.title: A Statue with Two Homelands
look.text: In a museum stands a stone Buddha carved about 1,800 years ago in what is now Pakistan. His calm face and topknot are Indian. But his robe falls in deep, realistic folds like a Greek statue, and his features look a little like Apollo. The sculptor had probably never been to Greece or to the Buddha's homeland.
look.prompt: How could one statue carry both Greek and Indian styles? What would have to travel along the roads for that to happen?

check.q: Which was the most important idea to travel the Silk Roads into China?
check.why: Buddhist monks came east with the caravans, and the religion spread across China and on to Korea and Japan.

check.q: What shows that Buddhism changed as it traveled?
choices: It stopped being practiced in India
Statues of the Buddha in Greek style and new schools in China
It was outlawed by the Han
check.why: Greek-influenced statues and new Chinese schools show blending with local cultures.

check.q: Which crop went west from China along the routes?
check.why: Peaches and apricots are native to China and traveled west; grapes, walnuts and alfalfa came east.

lessons.title: A Connected World
lessons.mainIdea: The same routes that spread goods and ideas also carried diseases, and by the 200s CE plague struck both Rome and Han China as both empires weakened.
reading: Trade routes connect people, and people carry germs. A disease that one population has lived with for generations can be deadly to another that has never met it. As caravans and ships tied Eurasia together, sicknesses moved along with them. Historians cannot always name the exact disease from ancient descriptions, but they can trace the outbreaks.

In 165 CE, Roman soldiers returning from a war in the east brought home a *plague* that spread through the empire for fifteen years. The doctor Galen described its fever and rash; many scholars think it was smallpox. Millions may have died, and some estimates put the loss at a tenth of the empire's population. A century later another wave hit. China's records show major epidemics in the same period, and the Han population fell sharply between the census of 2 CE and the counts of the late 100s.

Disease was not the only cause, but both great empires ran into deep trouble at about the same time. Han China collapsed in 220 CE into three kingdoms and then centuries of division. Rome survived its crisis of the 200s but never fully recovered in the west. Nomads pressed on both frontiers. Some historians argue that the very connections that made the empires rich also made them fragile.

The lesson is not that connection is bad. The Silk Roads gave the world paper, zero, Buddhism in East Asia and a thousand smaller gifts. It is that a connected world shares everything, good and bad, and needs ways to manage that. Illinois today ships corn to Asia and receives electronics, and O'Hare Airport links Chicago to every continent. The questions traders faced on the Silk Roads, about trust, fair exchange and risk, are still ours.

check.q: Why can a disease be deadlier in a new population?
choices: The new population has never met it and has no resistance
Traders carry more germs than soldiers
check.why: People who have never been exposed to a disease have no built-up resistance to it.

check.q: How do we know the Han population fell in the 100s CE?
choices: By comparing the census of 2 CE with later counts
check.why: Han officials counted the population, and later counts were much lower than the 2 CE census.

check.q: What is the lesson's main point about connection?
choices: Trade should be stopped to prevent disease
Rome and China should have stayed separate
Connection spreads both good things and dangers, so it must be managed
Only Buddhism spread along the roads
check.why: The Silk Roads brought paper, zero and religions as well as plague; the point is that a connected world shares everything.

review.q: What did Ashoka do after the Kalinga war?
choices: Burned the books of the scholars
Turned to Buddhism and announced rule by dharma
review.why: Horrified by the suffering, Ashoka carved edicts urging compassion and respect for all religions.

review.q: Which idea did Buddhism reject from the Indian society around it?
review.why: Buddhism kept karma and rebirth but opened its path to all, regardless of caste.

review.q: What was the most important mathematical gift of Gupta India?
review.why: Indian scholars developed place-value numbers with zero, which spread through the Arab world to Europe.

review.q: Which of these did the First Emperor of Qin do?
choices: Standardized writing, coins, measures and cart widths
Sent Zhang Qian to the west
review.why: Shi Huangdi unified China in 221 BCE and imposed one standard for writing and measures.

review.q: How did the Han choose officials, at least in principle?
choices: By inheritance from father to son
By recommendation and testing on Confucian learning
review.why: The Han began testing candidates on Confucian texts, the root of the later examination system.

review.q: What did Confucius say was most important for a state to keep?
review.why: Asked what to give up first, he said soldiers, then food, but never the people's trust.

review.q: Why did goods change hands many times along the Silk Roads?
choices: The Han forbade foreigners to enter China
No single trader traveled the whole distance
Camels could only walk a hundred miles
review.why: Merchants covered one stretch each, selling to the next group of traders at oasis markets.

review.q: Which of these traveled the Silk Roads besides trade goods?
review.why: Buddhism, paper, crops like peaches and grapes, and plague all moved along the routes.
